content: Twins are a type of multiple birth where a mother gives birth to two offspring from the same pregnancy. These twins can be of the same or opposite sex. The term multiples refers to more than one offspring from a single pregnancy, such as triplets, which involve three offspring. A single fetus in the womb is referred to as a singleton. Human twins are two individuals who shared the uterus during a single pregnancy and are typically born in close succession, though this is not always the case. Due to the limited size of the uterus, multiple pregnancies are less likely to reach full term compared to singleton pregnancies. Twin pregnancies, on average, last 37 weeks, which is three weeks shorter than full-term pregnancies. Premature births can lead to health complications for the babies, so twin births are often managed with special precautions. Twins can be classified as either monozygotic (identical) or dizygotic (fraternal). There are five common variations of twinning. The three most frequent types are fraternal twins: male-female twins (the most common, accounting for about 40% of all twins), female fraternal twins, and male fraternal twins. The remaining two types are identical twins: female identical twins and male identical twins, with male identical twins being the least common. Male singletons are slightly more common than female singletons by about 5%, but males are more susceptible to in-utero death. This higher mortality rate among male fetuses results in female twins being more common than male twins. A rare type of twinning, known as polar body twinning, occurs when one egg is fertilized by two different sperm, resulting in half-identical twins. This phenomenon was hypothesized and may have recently been proven to exist. Fraternal twins, also called dizygotic or biovular twins, occur when two separate eggs are fertilized by two different sperm cells and are implanted in the uterine wall simultaneously. These twins form two zygotes and are genetically similar to regular siblings, sharing about 50% of their DNA. Fraternal twins may look very similar or very different and can be of the same or different sexes. They are essentially siblings who happen to be the same age. Studies suggest a genetic basis for fraternal twinning, but only the female partner influences the likelihood of fraternal twins, as the male cannot cause the release of more than one ovum. Fraternal twinning rates vary by region, with rates as low as 6 per 1,000 births in Japan and as high as 14 or more per 1,000 in some African countries. Older mothers, particularly those over 35, are more likely to have fraternal twins. The use of fertility treatments has significantly increased the rate of fraternal twins, as seen in places like New York City, where twin births rose markedly between 1995 and 2004. Identical twins, or monozygotic twins, result from a single fertilized egg (zygote) that splits into two separate embryos. These twins share identical DNA but may have differences in traits and physical appearance due to environmental factors both in and outside the womb. Monozygotic twinning is not considered hereditary but rather a random anomaly, occurring at a rate of about 3 in 1,000 deliveries worldwide. Identical twins may develop separate placentas and sacs if the zygote splits very early (within the first two days after fertilization), known as dichorionic-diamniotic (di/di) twins. If the split occurs later, they may share a placenta but have separate sacs, called monochorionic-diamniotic (mono/di) twins. In rare cases, the split happens late enough to result in shared placentas and sacs, known as monochorionic-monoamniotic (mono/mono) twins. Extremely late splitting can lead to conjoined twins, who share body structures or organs. Mono/mono twins have a high in-utero mortality rate of about 60%, often due to cord entanglement, while conjoined twins face significant complications due to shared organs. Mono/di twins have a mortality rate of about 25%, primarily due to twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, while di/di twins have the lowest mortality risk at about 9%. Monozygotic twins are usually the same sex and look very similar, though they do not have identical fingerprints. Over time, lifestyle choices and environmental influences can make identical twins less alike. Genetically, the children of identical twins are half-siblings rather than cousins. If two sets of identical twins marry each other, their children would be genetic full siblings. The likelihood of monozygotic twinning appears to be a random event and is uniformly distributed across populations worldwide, unlike fraternal twinning, which varies by region and ethnicity. Studies of identical twins raised in different environments have shown that they often share similar personality traits, mannerisms, job choices, attitudes, and interests, supporting the idea that many behaviors are influenced by genetics. Identical twins have identical DNA, but environmental factors throughout their lives affect which genes are activated or deactivated, a process known as epigenetic modification. Research has shown that epigenetic differences between identical twins increase with age. Twins who have lived apart show the greatest differences, but certain traits, such as IQ and personality, become more similar as twins age, highlighting the role of genetics in human characteristics and behavior. A new theory suggests that identical twins form when an embryo collapses and splits its progenitor cells, dividing the same genetic material into two separate sides of the embryo, eventually developing into two fetuses. This research, presented in 2007, also explains why in-vitro fertilization (IVF) techniques are more likely to result in twins. Natural conception results in about 3 pairs of twins per 1,000 deliveries. Rare forms of twinning include semi-identical twins, where an unfertilized egg splits into two identical ova, each fertilized by different sperm. This results in twins with identical maternal genes but different paternal genes, creating chimeric individuals. Another rare phenomenon is heteropaternal superfecundation, where fraternal twins have different fathers due to eggs being fertilized at different times. Fraternal twins from biracial couples can sometimes exhibit differing ethnic and racial features. In extremely rare cases, monozygotic twins can be born with opposite sexes due to chromosomal abnormalities. Conjoined twins occur when a single zygote fails to completely separate, resulting in twins joined at birth. This condition occurs in about 1 in 50,000 pregnancies. Surgical separation of conjoined twins depends on the extent of shared organs or structures, with shared vital organs posing significant challenges. Chimerism occurs when an individual has cells from their twin or mother, leading to mosaicism in skin coloration or other features. Parasitic twins involve one twin failing to develop completely and acting as a parasite to the other. Partial molar twins occur when one zygote becomes cancerous, endangering the viable twin. Twins are more likely to have low birth weights and be born prematurely compared to singletons. Throughout their lives, twins tend to be smaller on average than singletons. Identical twins sharing a placenta can develop twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, where blood is unevenly distributed between the twins, endangering both. Twin studies are valuable for understanding the influence of genetics versus environment on human traits. Identical twins raised apart are particularly sought after for these studies. Rare patterns of twinning, such as superfecundation and superfetation, are exceedingly uncommon but have been documented. Twins are also common in many animal species, with some, like armadillos, regularly producing identical offspring.
